newsitem.title: USA: Trade uncertain over size of U.S. soybean supply.
newsitem.headline: Trade uncertain over size of U.S. soybean supply.

text.p: There is vast disagreement over the size of U.S. soybean supplies, and the uncertainty is causing market volatility, participants at a meeting of the National Insitute of Oilseed Products said.
"Everybody is watching that carryout, and when we don't see the Brazil crop, the market reacts," Jerry Gidel, Chicago-based analyst with Dean Witter said.
Gidel referred to Thursday's rally in Chicago Board of Trade soybean futures, where May soybeans soared as high as 28 cents per bushel in response to strong U.S. weekly export figures.

Much attention has been given the U.S. Department of Agriculture's 1996/97 scant soybean carryout of 140 million bushels, but some at the meeting also cast doubt on the size of the government's beginning stocks as well.
"During the month of September, it was like pulling teeth buying soybeans," said one crushing manager from the eastern Corn Belt.
USDA has forecast 1996/97 beginning stocks at 183 million bushels, but the crusher said based on his difficulty buying beans, he felt the carryin was closer to 150 million bushels.
But another crusher from the western Corn Belt said that supplies of soybeans have been readily available at his crushing facility.
"We didn't see that phenomenon in the West," the crusher said. "Beans are easy to buy when you get them up around $8.00 (per bushel)," he said.
Many in the trade had looked for an onslaught of soybean shipments from Brazil's new crop to pressure U.S. prices as early as the beginning of March.

However, the pace of exports from South America has been slow so far, and now some in the trade say that it will be April before the U.S. begins to lose a significant amount of export business to Brazil.
"We should see a continuing weakening basis as the South American crops come on line," said one analyst. "The key to this market is going to be April's crush and export news."

An informal survey of meeting participants showed that most believe the Brazilian soybean crop will come in near 27.5 to 28 million tonnes, and the Argentine crop will range from 12.75 to 13.50 million tonnes.
USDA has forecast the Brazilian soybean crop at 27 million tonnes and the Argentine soybean crop at 13.50 million tonnes.
Because of the U.S.'s historically low soybean supplies, large South American crops will be needed to meet world demand, meeting participants said.
